title: A Leader Can Be Popular and Wrong
paragraphs: A Leader Can Be Popular and Wrong
The crowd was roaring.
Voices rose like thunder. Approval flowed. The people were united. The leader stood at the center of it all, celebrated, admired, affirmed.
And yet heaven was grieved.
That may be one of the most uncomfortable truths in all of Scripture.
Popularity has never been proof of righteousness.
Applause has never been evidence of truth.
A leader can be admired by millions and still be walking in rebellion against God.
A leader can have influence, charisma, authority, talent, intelligence, vision, success, and a devoted following while simultaneously leading people away from the heart of the Lord.
We live in an age where numbers are often mistaken for anointing. Followers become substitutes for faithfulness. Visibility becomes confused with holiness. Influence becomes confused with obedience.
Yet the Bible repeatedly confronts us with a sobering reality:
God does not measure leaders the way people do.
The prophet Samuel learned this lesson when searching for Israel's next king.
The Lord told him:

“Man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart.”
(1 Samuel 16:7)
The Hebrew word for heart here is לֵבָב (levav), meaning the inner person, the true center of thoughts, desires, motives, and character.
Human beings often evaluate what can be seen.
God evaluates what cannot.
That truth should shake every leader.
And every follower.
Because sometimes the most dangerous leader is not the obviously corrupt one.
It is the admired one.
The one everyone loves.
The one nobody questions.
The one whose popularity becomes a shield against accountability.
Israel experienced this tragedy firsthand.
Aaron was respected.
Trusted.
Established.
He was Moses' brother.
The high priest.
A spiritual authority.
Yet when the people demanded an idol, Aaron gave them one.
Exodus records one of the most shocking leadership failures in Scripture.
The people wanted a visible god.
Something they could touch.
Something they could control.
Instead of standing firm, Aaron surrendered to public pressure.
He collected their gold.
Fashioned a golden calf.
And led the people into sin.
The crowd approved.
The nation celebrated.
The people worshiped.
Yet God's anger burned.
Aaron was popular.
Aaron was respected.
Aaron was wrong.
The lesson remains painfully relevant.
Leadership is tested not when people agree with you.
Leadership is tested when obedience to God becomes unpopular.
Anyone can stand with truth when truth is celebrated.
Faithful leaders stand with truth when truth costs them something.
Jesus Himself confronted this reality.
During His earthly ministry, crowds followed Him everywhere.
Thousands gathered to hear Him teach.
People wanted miracles.
Healing.
Provision.
Excitement.
Yet Jesus refused to shape His message around public approval.
In John 6, after delivering difficult teaching, many followers walked away.
The Greek text says:

ἀπῆλθον εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω
(apēlthon eis ta opisō)
Literally:
"They went back."
"They turned away."
The crowds shrank.
The applause faded.
The excitement disappeared.
Jesus did not change the message to keep the audience.
He let them leave.
Because truth was more important than popularity.
Faithfulness was more important than influence.
Obedience was more important than acceptance.
That principle is almost foreign in modern culture.
Today leaders are often tempted to tell people what they want to hear.
The prophet Jeremiah warned about this danger centuries ago.
False prophets repeatedly proclaimed:

"שָׁלוֹם שָׁלוֹם"
(shalom shalom)
“Peace, peace.”
When there was no peace.
They comforted people without confronting sin.
They offered reassurance without repentance.
They gave encouragement without truth.
The people loved it.
God condemned it.
Not every comforting voice is a godly voice.
Not every popular message is a biblical message.
Not every admired leader is leading people toward Christ.
Sometimes people follow leaders because they make them feel good.
Jesus calls us to follow leaders who help us become holy.
Those are not always the same thing.
The Lord repeatedly warned Israel about leaders who gathered followers while drifting from God.
Ezekiel spoke against shepherds who fed themselves rather than the flock.
Micah rebuked leaders who distorted justice.
Isaiah confronted rulers who honored God with their lips while their hearts remained far away.
Again and again Scripture reminds us that leadership is not measured by popularity.
It is measured by faithfulness.
The greatest example is Jesus Himself.
No leader in history was more righteous.
Yet no leader in history was more rejected.
The same crowd that cried “Hosanna” eventually shouted “Crucify Him.”
Public opinion changed.
Truth did not.
The Messiah remained the Messiah whether people applauded Him or condemned Him.
That reality should deeply challenge us.
Many believers spend enormous energy asking:
“What do people think of me?”
Far fewer ask:
“What does God think of me?”
One question builds a reputation.
The other determines eternity.
The Apostle Paul understood this tension.
Writing to the Galatians, he asked:
“Am I now seeking the approval of man, or of God?”
The Greek word for approval is πείθω (peithō), carrying the idea of winning favor or persuading others.
Paul understood something every Christian leader must learn.
The pursuit of human approval eventually collides with obedience to God.
Sooner or later a choice must be made.
And every leader reveals whom they truly serve by what they choose when that collision occurs.
This is not merely a warning for pastors, teachers, or public figures.
It applies to parents.
Employers.
Managers.
Politicians.
Ministry volunteers.
Influencers.
Business owners.
Anyone entrusted with influence.
Every one of us leads someone.
And every one of us faces the temptation to exchange truth for approval.
The frightening reality is that crowds can be wrong.
Entire cultures can be wrong.
Entire generations can be wrong.
History proves this repeatedly.
But God's Word remains unchanged.
Isaiah declared:
“The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever.”
Forever means forever.
Not until society disagrees.
Not until culture evolves.
Not until truth becomes inconvenient.
Forever.
Perhaps the most dangerous question a leader can ask is:
“How can I keep everyone happy?”
A far better question is:
“How can I remain faithful to Christ?”
One creates popularity.
The other creates discipleship.
One builds a platform.
The other builds a legacy.
One gathers applause.
The other hears:
“Well done, good and faithful servant.”
That is the voice every believer should long to hear.
Because there is coming a day when followers, influence, likes, status, recognition, titles, awards, and public admiration will all disappear.
Only Christ will remain.
Only truth will remain.
Only eternity will remain.
And on that day, no leader will be evaluated by popularity polls.
No one will be judged by audience size.
No one will stand before God carrying social influence as a defense.
The only question that will matter is faithfulness.
Were we faithful to Christ when obedience was costly?
Were we faithful when truth was unpopular?
Were we faithful when compromise seemed easier?
Were we remain loyal to Jesus when the crowd moved in another direction?
That question reaches beyond leadership and into every human heart.
Because each of us follows someone.
And before we follow any leader, we must first follow Christ.
Not because He is popular.
Not because culture approves.
Not because the crowd agrees.
But because He is Lord.
The greatest scandal in history was not that sinful humanity rejected Jesus.
The greatest scandal was that God used that rejection to accomplish salvation.
At Calvary, what appeared to be defeat became redemption.
What looked like failure became victory.
What looked like the end became a new beginning.
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
This is the beauty of grace.
This is why every broken story can be rewritten.
Because Jesus specializes in taking what seems ruined and transforming it into something redeemed.
From rebellion to restoration.
From shame to forgiveness.
From death to life.
Maybe this article exposed something uncomfortable.
Maybe it revealed places where approval has become more important than obedience.
Maybe it uncovered leaders you've followed too closely.
Maybe it exposed areas where you've been leading for applause instead of faithfulness.
If so, don't ignore that conviction.
Bring it to Christ.
His grace is greater than your failure.
His mercy is deeper than your compromise.
His cross is sufficient for your repentance.
And His resurrection power is still transforming hearts today.
Be honest. This hit harder than many expected.
Someone you know may desperately need this reminder today.
Supporting the mission helps expand Gospel-centered content that reaches hearts, strengthens believers, and points people to Jesus Christ around the world.
One day the crowd's voice will disappear, but the voice of Jesus will still be calling your name.
